text: The United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has filed an annual report pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, under Form 10-K. The registrant, The AES Corporation, is incorporated in the state of Delaware and has an IRS Employer Identification Number of 54-1163725. Its principal executive offices are located at 4300 Wilson Boulevard, Arlington, Virginia 22203, and its telephone number is (703) 522-1315. The company’s common stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol AES, and its corporate units trade under the symbol AESC. The AES Corporation is classified as a well-known seasoned issuer and is not required to file reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Act. It has filed all required reports during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to these filing requirements for the past 90 days. The company has submitted electronically all Interactive Data Files required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T. It is designated as a large accelerated filer and has not elected not to use the extended transition period for financial accounting standards. The registrant has filed a report on and received an attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. There are no restatements of previously issued financial statements or corrections of errors requiring a recovery analysis of incentive-based compensation for executive officers. The company is not a shell company. As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates was approximately $14.03 billion, based on a closing sale price of $21.01 per share on the New York Stock Exchange. The number of shares outstanding of the company’s common stock, par value $0.01 per share, as of February 27, 2023, was 668,824,617. Portions of the registrant’s 2023 Proxy Statement are incorporated by reference in Parts II and III of the report. The document includes a Table of Contents with a Glossary of Terms, and the report covers various sections including Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Market for Common Equity, Selected Financial Data, Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations, Market Risk, Financial Statements, and related notes. Additionally, the report includes disclosures on changes in accountants, controls and procedures, and other information.

The 2022 Annual Report includes various financial notes and disclosures, such as Note 24 on Held-for-Sale and Dispositions, Note 25 on Acquisitions, Note 26 on Earnings Per Share, Note 27 on Risks and Uncertainties, Note 28 on Related Party Transactions, Note 29 on Selected Quarterly Financial Data (Unaudited), and Note 30 on Subsequent Events. It also covers specific sections including Item 9 on Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants, Item 9A on Controls and Procedures, Item 9B on Other Information, and Item 9C on Foreign Jurisdictions Preventing Inspections. Part III includes Item 10 on Directors, Executive Officers, and Corporate Governance, Item 11 on Executive Compensation, Item 12 on Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management, Item 13 on Certain Relationships and Related Party Transactions and Director Independence, and Item 14 on Principal Accountant Fees and Services. Part IV, Item 15, contains Exhibits and Financial Statement Schedules. The report defines key terms such as ACED, AES, Adjusted EPS, Adjusted PTC, AFUDC, AIMCo, ANEEL, AOCL, ARO, ASC, BACT, BESS, BOT, CAA, CAMMESA, CCEE, CCGT, CCR, CDPQ, CECL, CEO, CFE, CFO, CO, COD, CSAPR, CWA, DG, DPL, DPP, EPA, EPC, ERCOT, ESP, EU, EURIBOR, EVN, FERC, Fluence, FONINVEMEM, FPA, FX, GAAP, GHG, GILTI, GSF, GW, GWh, HLBV. The report defines "AES," "the Company," "us," or "we" as referring to The AES Corporation and all of its subsidiaries and affiliates, while "The AES Corporation" and "Parent Company" refer only to the parent holding company, excluding subsidiaries and affiliates. Forward-looking statements are included in the report and are considered within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially due to factors such as the economic climate in operating regions and China, fluctuations in electricity prices and the effectiveness of risk management practices, changes in fuel prices and availability (including coal, gas, and transportation), access to financial markets and capital costs, inflation, demand for power, interest rates, and foreign exchange rates, the ability to meet debt obligations and manage liquidity, the receipt of funds from subsidiaries, and changes in corporate or subsidiary credit ratings.

AES is a global energy company founded in 1981, committed to delivering greener, smarter energy solutions and improving lives through innovation and operational excellence. The company is an industry leader in advancing zero and low-carbon energy solutions to achieve the Paris Agreement’s net-zero emissions goal by 2050. AES focuses on partnering with large corporations transitioning to carbon-free electricity, as evidenced by being recognized in 2022 by BNEF as the #1 global clean energy developer for corporations. In 2022, the company signed long-term contracts for 5.2 GW of renewable power, increasing its project backlog—comprising signed but not yet operational projects—to 12.2 GW, which serves as the foundation for future growth. A key element of its strategy is customer collaboration and co-creation, enabling tailored energy solutions that enhance customer satisfaction and allow bilateral partnerships beyond traditional bidding processes. This approach led to innovations such as agreements to supply 24/7 carbon-free energy for global data centers and a partnership with Air Products to develop and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility in the United States. AES also supports major mining companies in South America in reducing emissions through its Green Blend offering, which integrates renewable energy with thermal power to lower emissions. In its utility operations, AES promotes a Just Transition by retiring coal generation, such as at AES Indiana, where coal operations will be fully retired by the end of 2025, while adding new renewables and natural gas. The company expanded its development pipeline from 55 GW in January 2022 to 64 GW by the end of 2022 through acquisitions and increased investment in land acquisition and permitting. To mitigate supply chain risks, AES secured supplier arrangements for late-stage projects using its scale and advanced planning. A significant portion of its capital expenditures through 2025 will be allocated to renewable energy development. AES also operates AES Next, a business and technology incubator focused on identifying innovative technologies and business opportunities that support greener energy solutions. In 2022, the company signed 5,153 MW of long-term contracts. The company’s operations and future performance are subject to a range of risks, including market price risk, fuel availability and transportation, financial market conditions, inflation, interest rates, foreign exchange rates, liquidity and debt covenants, dividend and fund receipt capabilities, credit ratings, asset purchase and sale terms, competitive dynamics, facility operations, maintenance costs, contract performance, weather and natural disasters, pandemics, supply chain disruptions, capital availability, renewable project success, government incentives, environmental, social, and governance performance, technological advancements, customer trends, joint venture performance, rate treatment, regulatory changes, environmental laws, tax laws, litigation, acquisition performance, insurance, pension plan funding, asset impairments, accounting standards, internal controls, talent retention, cyber-attacks, and data privacy. These factors, along with others detailed in Item 1A.—Risk Factors and subsequent filings, should not be considered a comprehensive list of potential risks. AES undertakes no obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether due to new information or future events.

Our renewable growth strategy focuses on ensuring and enabling future growth by significantly expanding our pipeline of development projects, which increased from 55 GW in January 2022 to 64 GW by the end of 2022 through acquisitions and greater investment in development activities such as securing land and advancing permitting and interconnection processes. For late-stage projects, we secured supplier arrangements to prevent delays caused by industry shortages, leveraging our scale, existing supplier relationships, and advanced planning. A large portion of our expected capital expenditures through 2025 will be allocated to renewable project development. We are also actively developing and incubating new technologies that deliver value today and will support future business growth, recognizing the rapid changes in the energy industry. At the core of our innovation strategy is AES Next, a business and technology incubator that identifies innovative technologies and business opportunities to advance leading-edge, greener energy solutions. In 2022, we signed 5,153 MW of renewables and energy storage under long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), including 2,553 MW of solar, wind, and energy storage in the United States. We completed the construction or acquisition of 1,943 MW of operating projects in the United States, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, Chile, and Colombia, primarily in wind, solar, and energy storage. Our backlog—comprising projects with signed contracts but not yet operational—stands at 12,179 MW, including 5,453 MW under construction and 6,726 MW with signed PPAs not yet under construction. We announced a partnership with Air Products to develop, build, own, and operate the largest green hydrogen production facility in the United States, which includes approximately 1.4 GW of wind and solar generation and electrolyzer capacity capable of producing over 200 metric tons per day (MT/D) of green hydrogen. The company also expects to announce internal management changes that will result in modifications to its financial reporting segments. Our generation portfolio consists of 32,326 MW, including operations from AES Indiana, and is diversified by fuel type. Key performance drivers include types of electricity sales agreements, plant reliability and flexibility, availability of generation capacity, fuel costs, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, fixed-cost management, and competition. Most generation businesses sell electricity under medium- or long-term contracts (two to five years or more than five years), with contracts for fuel-based generation structured to recover variable costs through pass-throughs or tolling arrangements. Contracts without fuel pass-throughs are typically hedged or supported by fuel or energy supply agreements, and many include capacity payments to cover fixed costs such as fixed O&M, debt service, and a return on capital, often denominated in the same currency as fixed costs. Contracts without significant fuel costs or capacity payments are based on long-term spot prices with negotiated pass-throughs to recover fixed and variable costs and provide a return on investment. We generally eliminate or reduce foreign exchange risk by matching revenue and expense currencies, including fixed costs and debt, and hedge a significant portion of exposure to interest rate changes. Project debt may include both fixed and floating rates. Some businesses receive regulated market-based capacity payments. In short-term sales, power and ancillary services are sold under contracts with average terms under two years, including spot sales in competitive markets or at regulated prices. These markets operate on merit order dispatch, where the least expensive generation facilities are dispatched first, and prices are typically set at marginal cost or bid price. These businesses are more sensitive to electricity price fluctuations. We provide a range of ancillary services, including voltage support, frequency regulation, and spinning reserves. Many short-term markets include regulated capacity markets, which provide additional revenue based on availability, priced based on new entrant costs and system reserve margin. Capacity payments are typically received based on plant availability. Contract and short-term sales incentivize plants to manage availability, efficiency, and flexibility. For thermal generation, fuel is a major cost component; we use fuel supply agreements or financial hedges to manage costs, with some contracts including indexation, and tolling arrangements where off-takers cover fuel supply and costs. In short-term sales, power is sold at market prices reflecting current fuel costs, and fuel is procured on a short-term basis to match sales. Fuel price volatility significantly impacts short-term project economics. Forty-six percent of our generation capacity is fueled by renewables—including hydro, solar, wind, energy storage, biomass, and landfill gas—without significant fuel costs. Thirty-two percent is fueled by natural gas, with the exception of plants in the Dominican Republic and Panama, which import liquefied natural gas (LNG); otherwise, we source gas from local suppliers. Twenty percent of our fleet is coal-fired; in the U.S., most coal is sourced domestically, while in non-U.S. plants and Puerto Rico, coal is sourced from international and local markets, with global sourcing used to maximize fuel procurement efficiency. To meet local market needs, the company uses gas supplied by local vendors in each region. Twenty percent of its generation fleet's capacity is coal-fired, with domestic coal sourced in the U.S., while in non-U.S. plants and in Puerto Rico, coal is obtained from a mix of international and local sources. The company leverages its global sourcing program to enhance fuel procurement purchasing power. Two percent of the generation fleet uses pet coke, diesel, or oil, with oil and diesel sourced locally at prices tied to international markets, and pet coke primarily sourced from Mexico and the U.S. Generation operations are influenced by seasonal weather patterns, leading to uneven operating margins throughout the year, as well as by weather variations such as temperature, solar and wind resources, and hydrological conditions, which affect output at renewable facilities. In competitive power markets, local economic activity impacts power demand and short-term prices. For businesses with long-term contracts, most fixed operations and maintenance (O&M) costs are recovered through capacity payments, though managing and reducing fixed costs over time remains a key driver of performance. In medium- or long-term contracts, competition is limited during the contract term; short-term sales, plant dispatch, and electricity prices are determined by market competition and local dispatch and reliability rules. The company’s utility businesses include AES Indiana and AES Ohio in the U.S. and four utilities in El Salvador, serving 2.6 million customers, with the two U.S. utilities also including 3,495 MW of generation capacity. AES Indiana, a fully integrated utility, owns and operates all facilities for generation, transmission, and distribution, while AES Ohio owns and operates only transmission and distribution facilities. In El Salvador, the distribution business faces limited competition due to market entry barriers, and large regulated customers can opt to become unregulated and purchase directly from generation or commercialization agents. Utilities generally sell electricity directly to end-users and bill them directly; key performance drivers include the regulated rate of return and tariff, seasonality, weather variations, economic activity, and service reliability. Utilities are subject to government regulation, which sets tariffs and service standards, allowing a regulated rate of return on assets based on the utility’s allowed regulatory asset base, capital structure, and cost of capital. The asset base reflects the amount of useful assets serving customers, and both the allowed return and asset base are critical to earning power. The regulated tariff recovers allowed operating expenses and fixed costs, including fuel and purchased energy costs, and may include pass-throughs of uncontrollable costs. Tariffs are periodically reviewed or reset by regulators, often based on usage levels, and in some regions, customers with high demand can bypass the tariff by contracting directly with generators or suppliers and paying non-bypassable fees for distribution system use. Utilities must manage costs to match those in the tariff to avoid non-recovery or reduced returns. Seasonality and weather variations also affect utility operations, with retail sales influenced by customer usage patterns, temperature deviations, and local economic conditions, including energy efficiency and distributed generation. Reliability standards, such as outage duration and frequency, are required, either explicitly with performance incentives or penalties or implicitly through meeting customer and regulator expectations. The company develops and constructs new generation facilities, with utility projects built or retrofitted in response to customer needs or regulatory changes, subject to regulatory approval for capital recovery and return on investment. For generation, development priorities focus on key growth markets where renewable energy is added to leverage global scale and synergies with existing operations. Investment decisions are based on strategic fit, project returns, financial profile, and a fair risk-adjusted return, compared to alternative capital uses such as debt repayment. In some cases, long-term output contracts are secured before construction begins to reduce equity contributions from The AES Corporation, with non-recourse project debt and other capital sources, including partners, used when commercially viable. Third parties typically manage construction, though the company’s construction management team oversees progress, budget, and adherence to safety, efficiency, and productivity standards. The company is organized into four market-oriented strategic business units (SBUs): US and Utilities (U.S., Puerto Rico, and El Salvador), South America (Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil), MCAC (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean), and Eurasia (Europe and Asia), led by SBU Presidents. The two primary lines of business are generation and utilities. Each SBU participates in generation, where the company owns or operates power plants to generate and sell electricity to utilities, industrial users, and intermediaries. The US and Utilities SBU also participates in utilities, where it owns or operates utilities to generate, purchase, distribute, transmit, and sell electricity to residential, commercial, industrial, and government customers within defined service areas. In certain cases, utilities also generate and sell electricity on the wholesale market. SBU performance is measured using Adjusted PTC, a non-GAAP metric. AES Indiana is an integrated utility that generates, transmits, distributes, and sells electric energy to retail customers in Indianapolis and surrounding areas in Indiana, serving approximately 971,000 people across about 528 square miles. It holds an exclusive right to provide electric service in this area and operates four generating stations—all located within Indiana. The largest, Petersburg, is coal-fired; AES Indiana retired 230 MW of Petersburg Unit 1 on May 31, 2021, and plans to retire 415 MW of Petersburg Unit 2 in 2023, resulting in a total of 630 MW of retired economic capacity at the station. AES Indiana intends to convert the remaining two coal units at Petersburg to natural gas by the end of 2025. The second-largest station, Harding Street, uses natural gas and fuel oil to power combustion turbines and includes a 20 MW battery-based energy storage unit that provides frequency response. Eagle Valley is a CCGT natural gas plant, and Georgetown is a small peaking station using natural gas combustion turbines. AES Indiana also meets customer energy needs through long-term contracts for 300 MW of wind-generated electricity and 94 MW of solar-generated electricity. In July 2021, AES Indiana entered into an agreement to acquire a 250 MW solar and 180 MWh energy storage facility, the "Petersburg Solar Project," which was amended in October 2022 and is now expected to be completed in 2025, subject to IURC approval. In December 2021, AES Indiana completed the acquisition of Hardy Hills Solar Energy LLC, including a 195 MW solar project, the "Hardy Hills Solar Project," which was amended in December 2022 and is now expected to be completed in 2024, subject to IURC approval. AES Indiana's financial performance is primarily influenced by retail demand, weather, and maintenance costs, as well as regulatory outcomes, changes in legislation or regulations, and the timely recovery of capital expenditures. The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) regulates AES Indiana’s services, rates, securities issuance, and other matters, setting tariff rates that include basic rates and approved charges, along with various adjustment mechanisms such as the Fuel Adjustment Charge, environmental compliance costs, RTO cost changes, wholesale sales margins, returns on eligible TDSIC investments, and demand-side management program recoveries. On October 31, 2018, the IURC approved a settlement increasing AES Indiana’s annual revenues by $44 million (3%), primarily due to costs from the Eagle Valley CCGT and other construction projects, with new rates effective December 5, 2018. This order, the most recent base rate order, provided customers with approximately $50 million in benefits over two years through rate adjustments. AES Indiana is a member of MISO, a regional transmission organization that manages a major energy and ancillary services market and dispatches generation assets to meet demand, with AES Indiana offering electricity in MISO’s day-ahead and real-time markets. Its development strategy includes capital expenditures for utility operations and environmental compliance, as well as discretionary investments to replace aging equipment or improve performance. The TDSIC statute (Senate Enrolled Act 560) allows cost recovery outside base rate proceedings for transmission, distribution, and storage projects aimed at safety, reliability, modernization, or economic development. Eligible projects must include a five-year to seven-year plan, and once approved by the IURC, 80% of eligible costs can be recovered via a periodic TDSIC rate adjustment mechanism, including a return on investment, AFUDC, post-in-service carrying charges, operations, maintenance, depreciation, and property taxes, with the remaining 20% deferred to the next base rate case. The TDSIC mechanism is capped at a two percent annual increase of total retail revenues. On March 4, 2020, the IURC approved AES Indiana’s seven-year TDSIC Plan, totaling $1.2 billion in eligible investments from 2020 through 2026. Beginning in June 2020, AES Indiana files annual TDSIC rate adjustments for returns on investments through March 31, with rates effective each November, and submits annual plan updates staggered by six months, filed each December. As of December 31, 2022, the total amount of equipment approved for TDSIC recovery was $324 million. In December 2022, AES Indiana filed its Integrated Resource Plan (IRP), which outlines its preferred resource portfolio for meeting future generation needs, representing the reasonable least cost option and a cleaner, more diverse energy mix. AES Indiana plans to transition its remaining coal units at Petersburg to natural gas by the end of 2025. Although AES Indiana has not yet filed for regulatory approvals from the IURC to convert Petersburg Units 3 and 4, it expects to file at the appropriate time. The company also intends to add up to 1,300 MW of wind, solar, and battery energy storage by 2027. As new technologies such as green hydrogen, small modular reactors, and carbon capture become cost-effective, AES Indiana will evaluate them in future planning processes. AES Indiana's 2019 Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) included the retirement of 230 MW of Petersburg Unit 1 on May 31, 2021, and a plan to retire 415 MW of Petersburg Unit 2 in 2023. In November 2021, the IURC approved the retirements, including the creation of regulatory assets for the net book value of Units 1 and 2 upon retirement, a method for amortizing those assets, and recovery of the assets through ongoing amortization in future rate cases. The order reserves all parties' rights regarding ratemaking treatment, including the proper rate of return and recovery mechanisms. In December 2021, AES Indiana completed the acquisition of the Hardy Hills Solar Project, a 195 MW solar project expected to commence operations in 2024, which received IURC approval in June 2021. In July 2021, AES Indiana executed an agreement to acquire the Petersburg Solar Project, a 250 MW solar and 180 MWh energy storage facility expected to commence operations in 2025, which also received IURC approval in November 2021. In December 2021 and 2022, AES Indiana received equity capital contributions of $275 million and $253 million, respectively, from AES and CDPQ on a proportional share basis to fund TDSIC and replacement generation projects. AES Ohio is a utility that transmits and distributes electricity to approximately 536,000 retail customers in a 6,000 square mile area of West Central Ohio and is subject to regulatory authority. AES Ohio has the exclusive right to provide transmission and distribution services and procures retail standard service offer (SSO) electric service through a competitive bid auction process. Previously, AES Ohio Generation was a primary subsidiary, but DPL has systematically exited this generation business, retiring and selling its last remaining operating asset in 2020. AES Ohio's financial results are primarily driven by retail demand and weather, as well as regulatory outcomes, changes in legislation or regulations, and timely recovery of transmission and distribution expenditures. AES Ohio is regulated by the PUCO for distribution services, retail rates, reliability, compliance with renewable energy and energy efficiency requirements, and other matters. The PUCO maintains jurisdiction over electricity delivery, SSO, and retail electric services. Customers can purchase power from a Competitive Retail Electric Service (CRES) provider or from their local utility under SSO rates, which are supplied by third parties through competitive bidding. Ohio law requires utilities to file either an Electric Security Plan (ESP) or MRO plan to establish SSO rates. On December 18, 2019, the PUCO approved AES Ohio's Notice of Withdrawal and reversion to its prior rate plan (ESP 1), which reinstated the non-bypassable RSC Rider, generating approximately $79 million in annual revenues. The OCC has appealed to the Ohio Supreme Court, challenging the reversion to ESP 1 and seeking a refund of RSC revenues from August 2021; a decision is pending, and if the appeal results in terms more adverse than the current ESP plan, it could materially affect AES Ohio's results of operations, financial condition, and cash flows. On September 26, 2022, AES Ohio filed its latest ESP ("ESP 4"), a comprehensive plan to upgrade its network, improve service reliability, enhance price stability, and invest in local economic development, including increased distribution infrastructure investments and a proactive vegetation management program. ESP 4 also includes proposals for new customer programs such as renewable options, electric vehicle programs, and energy efficiency initiatives for residential and low-income customers, and seeks to recover outstanding regulatory assets not currently in rates. AES Ohio did not propose continuing the Rate Stabilization Charge in ESP 4, which requires PUCO approval anticipated in 2023. On November 30, 2020, AES Ohio filed a new distribution rate case application with the PUCO to increase base rates to address rising material and labor costs and substantial investments in distribution infrastructure. AES Ohio has a cost of long-term debt of 4.4% on a rate base of $783 million and an equity of 9.999%, with a capital structure of 53.87% equity and 46.13% long-term debt. This increased cost will take effect when AES Ohio has a new electric security plan in place, which is anticipated in 2023. On October 23, 2020, AES Ohio entered into a Stipulation and Recommendation with the PUCO and various customer organizations regarding its Smart Grid Plan, findings that AES Ohio passed the Significantly Excessive Earnings Test (SEET) for 2018 and 2019, and that its current ESP 1 satisfies both the SEET and the more favorable in the aggregate (MFA) regulatory test. In June 2021, the PUCO issued an opinion and order accepting the stipulation as filed, and AES made a $150 million cash contribution in 2021 to improve infrastructure and modernize its grid while maintaining liquidity. Several rehearing applications were filed and denied on December 1, 2021, and the OCC appealed the final PUCO Order to the Ohio Supreme Court on December 6, 2021; this appeal remains pending. On January 23, 2020, AES Ohio filed with the PUCO requesting approval to defer its decoupling costs consistent with the methodology from its Distribution Rate Case; if approved, deferral would be effective December 18, 2019 and would reduce impacts from weather, energy efficiency programs, and changes in customer demand. An evidentiary hearing was held on May 4, 2021, and these amounts are included in the ESP 4 application and are proposed to be recovered in a new rider. AES Ohio plans to spend an estimated $1.2 billion on capital projects from 2023 through 2025, including spending under its Smart Grid Plan from the October 2020 Stipulation and other transmission and distribution projects. The approved Smart Grid Plan provides for a return on and recovery of up to $249 million of Phase 1 investments and recovery of operational and maintenance expenses through the existing Infrastructure Investment Rider for a four-year term, with an aggregate cap of $268 million on recoverable amounts, and acknowledges that AES Ohio may file a subsequent application with the PUCO within three years for Phase 2 of the Smart Grid Plan. These spending programs are contingent on successful regulatory outcomes in pending proceedings. AES Clean Energy, part of AES' U.S. renewables portfolio, is one of the top U.S. renewables growth platforms and offers innovative solutions based on cutting-edge technologies to accelerate customers' energy futures. The generation capacity of systems owned and/or operated under AES Clean Energy is 4,919 MW across the U.S., with 2,862 MW under construction, including 1,707 MW of solar, 639 MW of wind, and 516 MW of energy storage. AES Clean Energy has a 5.2 GW backlog of projects, most expected to come online by 2025. The adoption of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in 2022 is expected to significantly accelerate U.S. renewables growth, and AES plans to meet this demand with its 51 GW development pipeline. AES Clean Energy comprises AES Renewable Holdings, sPower, AES Clean Energy Development (ACED), and other renewable assets. ACED was formed on February 1, 2021, by merging specifically identified projects from sPower and AES Renewable Holdings, and serves as the development vehicle for all future U.S. renewable projects. Following the merger, ACED expanded through the acquisitions of the Valcour Intermediate Holdings wind platform and Community Energy, a U.S. solar developer. AES Clean Energy has grown organically, now employing more than 1,000 people compared to less than 500 at its formation in 2021, and its development pipeline has more than doubled. In February 2023, the company sold 49% of its indirect interest in a 1.3 GW portfolio of sPower's operating assets ("OpCo B"), including 17 solar projects and one wind project across six states, to Hannon Armstrong Sustainable Infrastructure Capital, Inc. Key financial drivers for AES Clean Energy include efficient construction and operation of renewable facilities under long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs), which guarantee energy prices, and substantial tax credits, especially with the IRA. In 2022, AES recognized $246 million of pre-tax contribution related to allocating tax credits to tax equity partners. Financial results are driven by wind and solar resource availability, facility availability, project growth, and tax credit recognition upon placement
